name: Authoritative lake boundary sources versus the OpenStreetMap proxy

identity.method_name: Comparison of authoritative Bengaluru lake-boundary sources (KTCDA, Survey of India, Karnataka Revenue Department RTC/village records, ISRO Bhuvan, National Wetland Atlas 2024, BBMP Lakes Monitoring System) against the project's OpenStreetMap multipolygon proxy
identity.core_idea: The project currently fences each lake using a single, non-legal, crowd-edited OpenStreetMap multipolygon held constant across all 7 years. This item checks whether any government or institutional source can replace that polygon with something that has actual legal/administrative standing (a recorded survey/revenue boundary) or better spatial accuracy, and whether a solo B.Tech student can actually obtain it -- as opposed to merely knowing it exists.
identity.official_dataset_ids: KTCDA: no published open dataset ID -- the Authority's statutory function (s.5(4) and s.6(1) of Karnataka Act 32/2014) is to 'take up environmental planning and mapping of tanks ... with the help of GIS,' but no corresponding public GIS product/API was found. Survey of India: 'Open Series Maps' (OSM, unrelated to OpenStreetMap), 1:50,000 scale, freely downloadable as georeferenced PDF/raster from onlinemaps.surveyofindia.gov.in; larger-scale (1:25,000 and finer) toposheets exist but are restricted. Karnataka Revenue Department: Bhoomi RTC / village Akarband-Tippan cadastral records, landrecords.karnataka.gov.in (no formal 'dataset ID'; records are keyed by district-taluk-hobli-village-survey number). ISRO Bhuvan: NRSC thematic 'Water Bodies' / 'Wetlands' vector and WMS layers, served from bhuvan.nrsc.gov.in (no single canonical product code found; layers are organised under the Bhuvan Thematic Services index). National Wetland Atlas 2024: Phase-2 National Wetland Inventory and Assessment (NWIA), Space Applications Centre (SAC)/ISRO, published March 2024, 1:12,500 scale, 20-class wetland typology, derived from Resourcesat-2/2A LISS-IV imagery (pre/post-monsoon 2018-2019); hosted/described via vedas.sac.gov.in. BBMP: 'Lakes Monitoring System,' lms.bbmpgov.in (a web application with per-lake report pages, e.g. lms.bbmpgov.in/viewlakenew/{id}; not a published dataset with an ID).

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: not applicable -- this item concerns the spatial reference (boundary) input, not an encroachment label. However it is the direct upstream dependency of legal_traceability for every other method in this project: whichever boundary is used to build the buffer fence (see B1) inherits that boundary's own legal standing or lack of it.
fit_to_project.input_required: A single, static (or, ideally, per-year, per-lake) polygon per lake in a metric CRS matching the project grid (EPSG:32643). The project already has an OSM multipolygon for this. What it lacks is any of the six candidate authoritative sources in a form a solo student can actually download and use as a drop-in replacement -- see legal_traceability below for the source-by-source finding.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: yes -- boundary acquisition is a per-lake (n=6), one-time task, independent of the 42-row tabular structure.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes -- none of the six candidate sources require encroachment labels; they are all raw boundary/reference data.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Mixed and source-dependent. Survey of India Open Series Maps (1:50,000, ~25-50 m planimetric accuracy) are coarser than the 20 m pixel grid and not fit for precise boundary delineation. The National Wetland Atlas 2024 at 1:12,500 scale is finer than 20 m and would in principle be adequate if obtainable. Karnataka RTC/village records give an exact legal extent (in acres/guntas) but the associated cadastral map (Akarband/Tippan) is typically a scanned, non-georeferenced or poorly georeferenced sheet, so converting it to a clean vector polygon at 20 m grid accuracy requires manual georeferencing work, not a direct download. Bhuvan's thematic water-body/wetland layers are nominally at similar resolution to the source LISS-IV/Resourcesat imagery (~5.8-23.5 m depending on product), broadly compatible with the 20 m grid.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: none -- this is reference geometry, not a label.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Directly targets the project's stated limitation that the OpenStreetMap boundary is 'NOT a legal boundary and carries no statutory standing' and is 'fixed across all 7 years' (project_constraints.lake_boundary). Replacing OSM with an authoritative source could, in principle, also help address limitation (2) (no growth signal) if a source published boundary revisions over time -- but no source found here publishes a multi-year boundary time series (see temporal_granularity).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: no -- a better boundary source only fixes where the fence sits, not what is happening to water/vegetation inside it; desilting still has to be handled downstream.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: no -- same reasoning as above; boundary source choice is orthogonal to the water-vs-hyacinth classification problem.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: Source-by-source finding, in order of how authoritative and how obtainable each actually is: (1) Karnataka Revenue Department RTC / Bhoomi (landrecords.karnataka.gov.in) -- THE most legally authoritative source in principle, since a tank's statutory extent is defined by its revenue/survey record (this is also what the 2025/2026 KTCDA buffer amendment measures FROM -- 'revenue boundary of the tank,' see B1). RTC text records (extent, kharab classification) are viewable and downloadable free, with no institutional login, by district/taluk/hobli/village/survey number; a certified i-RTC costs Rs 15. However, the RTC gives area and classification as TEXT, not a ready GIS polygon; the associated village map/Akarband is a scanned cadastral sheet that must be manually georeferenced to produce a usable vector boundary -- a real but learnable task for a solo student (a few days per lake, not an afternoon). This is corroborated by a primary source: the Karnataka High Court's own 2011 Lake Preservation Committee Report (Justice N.K. Patil Committee, 26.02.2011, pursuant to HC order dated 26.11.2010 in WP No. 817/2008) states verbatim that lake boundaries are established by 'survey ... as per the village map and records,' with 'boundary stones ... fixed ... to facilitate easy future re-survey,' recommending their corner coordinates be recorded by 'Differential Global Positioning System (GPS) of sub-meter accuracy,' and that 'Geographical Information System (GIS) is to be established for the lakes of Bangalore City' -- i.e. as of 2011 (and, on the evidence gathered here, still today) no ready-made authoritative digital GIS boundary layer existed; it was something to be built FROM revenue records by fieldwork, not downloaded. (2) Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority (KTCDA) -- statutorily the correct custodian and the body whose Act (s.6(1)) empowers it to 'survey, demarcate and make a map of tanks,' but no public-facing GIS portal, shapefile, or open dataset was found on ktcda.karnataka.gov.in (the site's own Act & Rules page returned a server error during this research); a formal written request to KTCDA is plausible but was not testable here and cannot be assumed to succeed within a B.Tech timeline. (3) Survey of India -- the classic reference for Indian topographic boundaries, but only its 1:50,000 Open Series Maps are freely downloadable (onlinemaps.surveyofindia.gov.in), and at that scale individual lake boundaries are not delineated with usable precision; large-scale (1:25,000 or finer) maps that would resolve a single lake are subject to the post-2021 restricted-map policy and require a formal application (Form O.57A), which is not a same-day self-service download and has no guaranteed approval timeline for a student project. (4) ISRO Bhuvan -- publishes thematic water-body/wetland WMS layers viewable in a browser or GIS client without login, and some LULC-type products are downloadable free after registration; however, no evidence was found of a bulk, ready-to-clip per-lake boundary vector download specific to Bengaluru's six named lakes; usable access is realistically WMS-viewer level, not a clean shapefile handoff. (5) National Wetland Atlas 2024 (SAC/ISRO, 1:12,500) -- the most spatially precise of the remote-sensing-derived sources and explicitly wetland-focused, but this research could not confirm a direct, login-free bulk shapefile/geodatabase download; the pattern from the earlier (2011) edition of the same Atlas was state-wise PDF books plus a Bhuvan map viewer, with vector data released to researchers/agencies on request rather than as an open self-serve download -- the 2024 edition's access model should be treated as materially the same until shown otherwise, i.e. [uncertain] whether a student can download it outright. (6) BBMP Lakes Monitoring System (lms.bbmpgov.in) -- a public-facing web app with a page per lake (e.g. Ulsoor, Chikkabellandur, Begur) showing status/report information; no boundary shapefile, KML, or coordinate export was found on the pages examined, and full data appears gated behind a registration/login flow for other functions (a 'register'/'login' page exists on the same domain); it should be treated as an operations/grievance dashboard, not a GIS boundary source. Net conclusion: none of the six sources gives a solo student a same-day, no-login, ready-to-use vector polygon that is simultaneously more legally authoritative than OSM AND easier to obtain than OSM. The one source with genuine legal standing and no-login access (Karnataka RTC/Bhoomi) requires real georeferencing labour to turn into a polygon; the sources with the best-looking GIS infrastructure (KTCDA, Bhuvan, National Wetland Atlas) each have an access gate (missing public portal, WMS-only, or on-request data) that this research could not get past without direct correspondence with the issuing agency.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: None of the six sources publish a multi-year boundary revision history usable for this project's 2019-2025 window: Survey of India toposheets are updated irregularly and on decades-long cycles (the Karnataka HC 2011 report itself cites 1972 as the 'last most authoritative' toposheet account for parts of Bangalore); the National Wetland Atlas 2024 edition is a single snapshot benchmarked to 2018-2019 imagery (its predecessor was a single 2011 snapshot benchmarked to circa 2006-2007); RTC/revenue records reflect the current recorded extent, not a historical time series, unless a student manually orders archived jamabandi records; Bhuvan and BBMP LMS reflect current status only. Any authoritative source adopted would therefore, like the current OSM proxy, have to be applied as a SINGLE static polygon across all 7 study years -- it would improve legal standing but would not, by itself, fix the 'one static boundary, no growth signal' limitation.

implementation.libraries: geopandas, shapely, fiona/pyogrio for vector I/O; QGIS (free) for manually georeferencing scanned Akarband/village maps and digitising a boundary from RTC records; rasterio/OWSLib if consuming Bhuvan WMS layers.
implementation.licence: RTC/Bhoomi records are Government of Karnataka public records, free to view; no explicit open-data licence statement was located, but factual land-record data of this kind is conventionally treated as public information for citation/research use. Survey of India Open Series Maps are released under Survey of India's own map policy (free download, attribution expected; large-scale maps are licence-restricted, not merely paid). Bhuvan/NRSC data terms require registration and generally restrict commercial redistribution but permit research use. National Wetland Atlas data licensing could not be confirmed in this research -- [uncertain]. KTCDA has no published licence because no public dataset was found. None of this is a blocking concern for an academic capstone as long as the source and any registration/attribution terms are disclosed.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial for using a ready vector file (seconds, CPU-only). Non-trivial in STUDENT TIME (not compute) for the RTC/Akarband path, which requires manual georeferencing in QGIS -- realistically a few hours to a day per lake depending on map quality and number of survey numbers making up the tank.
implementation.student_days: OSM (current baseline): 0 additional days. RTC/revenue-record path to a usable polygon: roughly 0.5-1.5 days per lake (record retrieval + georeferencing + digitising), so 3-9 days across the project's 6 lakes -- a real but bounded cost. KTCDA/Bhuvan/Wetland Atlas paths: effort is dominated by an unpredictable wait for an institutional data request or registration approval that this research could not verify would succeed at all within a capstone timeline; treat as 'unknown, possibly unobtainable' rather than a fixed day count.

evaluation.metrics: Not a predictive method. The relevant comparison metric across candidate boundary sources is positional/area agreement: overlay each obtainable boundary against the current OSM polygon and report IoU (intersection-over-union) and area difference in hectares per lake, to quantify how much the choice of boundary source alone moves the headline 'water area' or 'encroachment area' numbers.
evaluation.validation_protocol: A per-lake sensitivity comparison (not a train/test split): for whichever authoritative boundary is actually obtained (most plausibly the RTC-derived one), compute IoU against OSM for all 6 lakes and report the spread, rather than assuming the two are interchangeable.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Not a statistical-leakage concern in the ML sense; the analogous risk is silently swapping boundary sources between lakes (e.g. using a hand-digitised RTC boundary for one lake and OSM for another) without disclosing the inconsistency, which would make cross-lake comparisons within the project's own results non-comparable.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: Report boundary-source disagreement (IoU / hectare difference vs OSM) per lake as an explicit uncertainty band on any area-based result, since the boundary itself is now known to be a source of measurement uncertainty, not a fixed ground truth.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: not applicable -- no synthetic data is involved in acquiring or digitising a boundary.

evidence.published_performance: Not a performance-metric item. Documented specification figures: National Wetland Atlas 2024 -- 1:12,500 scale, 20-wetland-type classification, built from Resourcesat-2/2A LISS-IV pre/post-monsoon 2018-2019 imagery, published March 2024 by SAC/ISRO under Phase-2 NWIA (confirmed across multiple independent secondary sources describing the same SAC publication -- moderate-high confidence on the specification, [uncertain] on public download mechanics). Survey of India Open Series Maps -- 1:50,000, free PDF download (confirmed). KTCDA statutory GIS-mapping mandate -- s.5(4)/s.6(1) of Act 32 of 2014 (confirmed directly from the Act's own text, retrieved via PRS Legislative Research), but no corresponding live public dataset (unconfirmed / likely does not exist as an open product).
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: All six candidate sources are national or Karnataka-state products, applied here specifically to Bengaluru's BBMP/BDA-area lakes; no scale mismatch of the kind the project's own field definitions warn against (e.g. a nationwide product being read as validated for six lakes) -- the concern here is availability, not statistical generalisability.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: yes, all six sources are India-specific (several Karnataka-specific); the National Wetland Atlas and Bhuvan are the only pan-India products among them, but both include Bengaluru's lakes within their coverage. On whether a published Bengaluru lake-encroachment study used an authoritative boundary: no study located in this research was confirmed, from a directly quoted methodology section, to have used KTCDA, Bhuvan, the National Wetland Atlas, or BBMP LMS boundary data. The strongest available evidence points to IISc's Energy & Wetlands Research Group (T.V. Ramachandra and co-authors), whose Bengaluru lake/encroachment work is reported (via aggregated search results, not a directly confirmed quoted methods passage -- [uncertain]) to rely on Survey of India toposheets converted to GIS layers plus handheld/differential GPS ground survey of boundary corners -- i.e. the same 'survey from revenue/village records plus field GPS' approach the 2011 Karnataka High Court committee report itself recommends, not a ready-made download from any of the six candidate portals.
evidence.evidence_recency: National Wetland Atlas 2024 (March 2024) and the KTCDA Amendment Act 2025/2026 (18.02.2026, relevant to the 'revenue boundary' measurement definition referenced above) are both current as of this research (September 2026). The corroborating Karnataka High Court committee report on how lake boundaries are actually established is from 2011 and is used only to confirm that boundary determination has historically depended on manual survey of revenue records, not to claim a current-day figure; if no more recent confirmation that this practice has changed is found, this should be flagged as reliance on an older primary source for a practice-level (not legal-figure) claim.
evidence.primary_sources: Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority Act, 2014, ss.5(4), 6(1) (statutory GIS-mapping mandate), via PRS Legislative Research: https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_states/karnataka/2014/2014KR32.pdf ; Karnataka High Court Lake Preservation Committee Report (26.02.2011), on how boundaries are surveyed from village maps/records: https://data.opencity.in/dataset/46dffdd5-1b51-4a72-bdc0-41a0ec85c31c/resource/225ab3a3-e767-4b63-a406-7048712d6b46/download/0634635f-5928-4030-aaea-d125e488aec2.pdf ; BBMP Lakes Monitoring System: https://lms.bbmpgov.in/lake and per-lake pages such as https://lms.bbmpgov.in/viewlakenew/180 (fetch blocked by certificate error during this research; described from search-indexed content only -- [uncertain]); Bhuvan thematic data documentation: https://bhuvan.nrsc.gov.in/wiki/index.php/Thematic_Data ; National Wetland Atlas 2024 background: https://www.downtoearth.org.in/water/theres-a-pressing-need-for-a-dedicated-and-broad-based-national-wetlands-inventory-programme and https://vedas.sac.gov.in/en/National_Wetland_Inventory_and_Assessment_(NWIA)_Atlas.html ; Karnataka Bhoomi/RTC portal description: https://www.landeed.com/post/unlocking-rtc-record-of-rights-tenancy-and-crops-in-karnataka and the official portal landrecords.karnataka.gov.in ; Survey of India map access/restriction policy: https://onlinemaps.surveyofindia.gov.in/AboutPortal.aspx and https://indiadataatlas.deccanspatial.com/chapters/ch01-boundaries/soi/ ; IISc Energy & Wetlands Research Group (T.V. Ramachandra et al.) Bengaluru lake/encroachment work referencing Survey of India toposheets and handheld/differential GPS field survey as their boundary-verification method: https://wgbis.ces.iisc.ac.in/energy/water/paper/ETR101/encroachment.html (the specific methodology description could not be directly confirmed from a machine-readable methods section in this research -- [uncertain], based on aggregated search-result summaries rather than a verbatim quoted passage).

risk.failure_modes: (1) Assuming any of KTCDA/Bhuvan/National Wetland Atlas can simply be 'downloaded' the way OSM currently is -- the evidence gathered here says none of the three has a confirmed, login-free, ready-to-use vector download for named Bengaluru lakes; a student who budgets zero days for this will likely fail to obtain anything and fall back to OSM anyway, but late in the project. (2) Treating RTC/Bhoomi's textual area figures as a plug-in replacement for a polygon without doing the georeferencing work the raw record requires. (3) Mixing boundary sources across the six lakes inconsistently and not disclosing it. (4) Over-claiming legal standing for a boundary that was in fact only viewed on a web portal (e.g. Bhuvan's WMS viewer) rather than obtained as a citable, versioned dataset.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask 'is that lake boundary the legal one, and how do you know?' The honest, defensible answer established here is: the only source with genuine statutory/legal standing that a student can actually reach without institutional backing is the Karnataka Revenue Department's RTC/village record, and reaching a usable polygon from it costs real (though bounded) manual effort; every other 'official-sounding' source (KTCDA, Bhuvan, National Wetland Atlas, BBMP LMS) either has no confirmed open download or was not verifiable as obtainable within this research, and claiming otherwise without having actually completed a download will not survive a follow-up question.
risk.honest_expectation: For a solo B.Tech student on the stated timeline, the realistic outcome is one of two honestly reportable positions: (a) keep the OpenStreetMap polygon as the working boundary but explicitly upgrade the write-up's caveat -- state plainly that OSM has no statutory standing, that the one source which does (RTC/revenue boundary) is technically reachable but was not converted to a polygon within project time, and quantify the risk by digitizing at least one lake's RTC boundary as a spot-check against OSM (reporting the IoU/area difference for that one lake as evidence of how much this matters); or (b) invest the 3-9 student-days to hand-digitise RTC/Akarband boundaries for all 6 lakes and use that as the legally-grounded fence, explicitly documenting the manual georeferencing method as the 'authoritative boundary' methodology. A null result -- 'we checked five plausible official sources and could not obtain a downloadable boundary from four of them without an institutional login or a data request whose outcome we could not verify' -- is itself the most defensible and evidence-based finding this item can produce, and is preferable to overstating access that was not actually confirmed.

verdict.recommended_rank: consider-with-reasons -- do not assume any of the five 'official' portals (KTCDA, Survey of India large-scale, Bhuvan, National Wetland Atlas, BBMP LMS) will yield a usable boundary within project time; if legal traceability of the fence genuinely matters to the write-up, budget real days for a manual RTC/revenue-record-based digitisation of at least the project's largest or most-discussed lake(s) as a documented spot-check against OSM, and otherwise keep OSM with an explicit, upgraded caveat.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: None of KTCDA, Survey of India, Bhuvan, the National Wetland Atlas 2024, or the BBMP Lakes Monitoring System offers a confirmed, login-free, ready-to-use lake boundary a solo student can download to replace OpenStreetMap; the only source with real legal standing (Karnataka Revenue Department RTC/village records) is reachable but requires manual georeferencing effort, so this project kept the OSM polygon and disclosed its lack of statutory standing as an explicit limitation rather than overstating access to an 'official' boundary that could not actually be obtained.
